content:
Some thoughts on Dario’s post:

1. Dario does not actually address Gavin Baker’s account of what he said – something he could easily deny if it were inaccurate.

2. Dario claims his critics live in a “bubble” where all regulation equals regulatory capture. He calls this an overly simplified view and notes that “Many people outside this bubble think of regulation as something that constrains corporate power and benefits ordinary people.” This argument is a straw man. Of course treating all regulation as capture would be overly simplified – but almost no one holds that view. I have repeatedly argued for strong antitrust enforcement to keep industries competitive, especially Big Tech. If Anthropic continues toward monopoly or duopoly status, I would be among the first to demand those rules apply.

3. Regulatory capture is not vague or in the eye of the beholder. Nobel laureate George Stigler defined it as regulation acquired by an industry and designed and operated primarily for its benefit. Stigler challenged the traditional view that government regulation arises from a benevolent state protecting the public from market failures. Rather, industry groups have concentrated stakes and pour resources into influencing regulators, whereas the public’s stake is diffuse and unorganized. The revolving door between companies and the agencies that regulate them compounds the problem. Anthropic understands these dynamics: it has hired multiple senior Biden AI-policy officials and built a substantial government-affairs operation plus a network of aligned organizations to push its preferred frameworks at state and federal levels.

4. Dario has consistently pushed for a new federal agency to review and approve frontier models prior to release – a proposal framed variously as an “FDA for AI,” an “FAA for AI,” and most recently a “FINRA for AI.” I call it a “DMV for AI” because a review process modeled on the FAA or FDA (which takes years) or FINRA (which issues rules for a staid industry widely seen as protecting incumbents) will create long queues as AI models wait for testing and approval. This process will only become more labyrinthine as rules accumulate to prevent theoretical harms. This would handicap the U.S. relative to China, which will not adopt the same constraints. It would also undermine Anthropic’s own business model, whose pricing power depends on remaining ahead of open models. Whatever Dario states today, it is difficult to believe the company would simply accept outcomes that erase that advantage.

5. Anthropic is on track to become one of the most valuable companies in history, with the resources to navigate any approval process and shape the rules while competitors wait. Dario wants open models under heavier scrutiny – he has called them dangerous in Senate testimony, criticized them for not being centrally monitored or withdrawn, and linked them to IP theft. He says he has never sought a ban, but he could achieve a similar result by insisting that identical rules apply to both open and closed models. The U.S. risks becoming an island of costly closed models while the rest of the world races ahead with broader choice.

6. Dario acknowledges that AI is structurally centralizing but attributes this mainly to chips and scaling laws. Access to compute matters, but the deeper risk is who decides which capabilities are available to whom. His preferred pre-deployment testing and FAA/FINRA-style oversight would place that gatekeeping power in a federal bureaucracy working hand-in-glove with a small number of frontier labs – reinforcing centralization rather than countering it.

7. The second part of Dario’s post assumes we have amnesia about Anthropic’s well-orchestrated campaigns hyping AI fears. His May 2025 claim that AI would wipe out 50 percent of entry-level knowledge jobs within five years still lacks supporting evidence fifteen months later. Similarly Anthropic breathlessly promoted its heavily contrived “blackmail” study on 60 Minutes. Yet Dario blames public negativity on a long-standing loss of trust in institutions rather than his own messaging.

8. These narratives have done more than anything to shape public fear. People are left asking the same question Mark Zuckerberg posed: why race to build a future you describe in such negative terms? Thomas Sowell’s "The Vision of the Anointed" captures the mindset – elite intellectuals convinced that only they are enlightened enough to control the outcome. As Zuckerberg notes, concentrating power in the hands of an enlightened few has rarely produced the promised results; the practitioners turn out to be less enlightened in practice than in self-conception.

9. Gavin Baker summarized the disagreement cleanly on our pod: Dario believes frontier AI is too powerful to distribute; we believe it is too powerful to centralize. Dario appears to believe, sincerely, that safety and progress are best served by centralizing authority in a marriage of corporate and state power. The weight of human history gives us reason to fear that outcome.

content:
The most downloaded AI on earth is now Chinese.

Alibaba just gave away a model that matches Claude's flagship, and it literally runs on a $700 used graphics card.

The Qwen models crossed 3 BILLION downloads in six months.

Hugging Face counted 418 million downloads for Google this year, and 227 million for Meta.

Alibaba cleared more than four times both of them combined.

Then today it released Qwen3.8-27B under an Apache 2.0 license.

The model has 27 billion parameters, native vision, and a 262,000 token context window. Developers are running it locally on 17 gigabytes of memory, on used cards that cost a few hundred dollars.

Alibaba's own benchmark table claims it beats Opus 4.6 Max on computer use by 84.3 to 72.7, on mobile use by 81.9 to 62, and on visual math by 94.6 to 65.5. Those numbers come from the vendor and nobody has independently verified them yet, so treat them as a claim.

But the generation over generation jumps are harder to wave away:

On DeepSWE the score went from 13.3 to 42.2. On software engineering it went from 49.3 to 79.0. That happened in ONE release cycle.

And Apache 2.0 means anyone can download the weights, modify them, build products on them, sell those products, and never pay or ask permission. It cannot be revoked. Once the file is on your drive it is yours permanently.

3 billion downloads means those files already sit on machines in every country on Earth.

Alibaba could delete everything tomorrow and it would change nothing.

Washington spent 4 years building an export control regime around chips, model weights, and entity lists. Every piece of it assumes a chokepoint exists somewhere. A fab, a shipment, a company that can be told no.

But there is no chokepoint for a file that has already been copied three billion times.

And the copying compounds.

content:
Here is how to enable a 1M-token context window in Codex for GPT-5.6 Sol. 

Even though we have tuned the context limit in Codex to be set optimally when it comes to performance and cost, this is a common ask, so here it is documented.

A larger context window lets Codex retain more code, tool output, and conversation history before summarizing older material. You need a model that supports it. And GPT-5.6 Sol, for example, has a documented 1,050,000-token window. 

Open ~/.codex/config.toml and add or update these settings at the top level, before any [section] headers:

```
model = "gpt-5.6-sol"
model_context_window = 1000000
model_auto_compact_token_limit = 900000
```

The first setting selects the model. The second tells Codex to use a one-million-token context budget. The third starts automatic history compaction around 900,000 tokens, leaving some headroom. Restart Codex client and start a new session after saving. 

To try the configuration for a single CLI session without changing your defaults:

```
codex -m gpt-5.6-sol \
  -c model_context_window=1000000 \
  -c model_auto_compact_token_limit=900000
```

Have fun, but also know that we tuned the default carefully!

For years, labs like OpenAI and Google have bragged about near-perfect scores on benchmarks like GSM8K. They claimed AI had mastered logical problem-solving.

When Apple changed the simple numbers inside a basic word problem, model accuracy plummeted. The AI wasn't solving the math. It was relying on pattern matching from its training data.

It was guessing based on familiarity, not reasoning.

Then they ran the test that exposed the illusion entirely.

They added a single, irrelevant clause to a math problem. Just a sentence of background text that looked important, but had zero impact on the actual calculation.

Every single frontier model, from ChaTGPT to Claude, suffered massive performance drops.

Some crashed by up to 65%.

Just by adding a piece of noise that a seven-year-old child could easily ignore.

The conclusion is blunt.

Current AI models do not possess genuine logical reasoning. They do not understand math. They are sophisticated mimicry engines replicating the shape of human logic without actually thinking.

When the pattern is clean, they look like geniuses.

The moment you introduce a minor twist, a variable change, or a distraction, the illusion shatters.

title:
This is probably everything you need to know about the biggest AI subscriptions right now.

All of it comes from actual daily use. I'm a heavy user, I pay for these myself, and a few of them I've paid
content:
This is probably everything you need to know about the biggest AI subscriptions right now.

All of it comes from actual daily use. I'm a heavy user, I pay for these myself, and a few of them I've paid for annually. None of this is based on benchmarks or a handful of prompts. I've used them hard enough to know what they're actually good at, and how fast the limits show up.

SuperGrok

The model is excellent. Fast, high quality output, and in my experience it rarely hallucinates. It follows instructions well and works especially well as an orchestrator.

You also get image and video generation, but the real advantage is direct access to X. If you run a business, follow markets, track trends, or need to know what people are reacting to right now, that access is worth real money.

It's also very good with PDFs. The output usually comes out clean and well designed.

For coding I like it for repeated PR work, fixing conflicts, and anything where I want strong execution without waiting forever.

The downside is the predictable one. The usage limits are hard to justify at this price.

Best harness for me: Grok Build.

MiniMax Token Plan

The most generous and transparent subscription I use. They tell you how many tokens you're paying for, and that's what you get. No mystery around usage. In practice it often feels close to unlimited.

At $20 I still think it's the king of that price range for light to medium work, image generation, music, computer use, and general creative work.

M3 is one of my favorite models for web development. It builds interfaces that actually look beautiful.

And speed? Probably the fastest open model I've used from an official provider. Ridiculously responsive.

The weaknesses are instruction following and long horizon work. It drifts, misreads constraints, or starts hallucinating once the task gets big.

Best experience for me: Hermes or MCode.

GLM Coding Plan

Harder to judge, because the experience seems to change a lot from one user to another.

When it behaves normally it can be extremely generous. Mine has mostly been good, and the Max tier gives you a lot for the price. In raw coding value it can beat Codex or Claude.

But plenty of users complain that cache hits appear to count against usage. If that happens to you, the value of the plan collapses.

The model itself is excellent on large codebases and very good at UI/UX work.

The weakness is speed. It's slow, and in general intelligence I wouldn't put it at the top of the market.

For long horizon work I prefer CodeCode. For normal daily tasks, Zcode.

Also watch the four hour peak window where usage can cost 3x. If those hours land on your workday, this subscription may simply not make sense for you.

ChatGPT

If all you want is the best general chatbot subscription, ChatGPT is still the easiest one for me to recommend.

The normal ChatGPT side feels basically unlimited. It's extremely fast, very good at research, useful for planning, solid at checking facts and prices and practical details, and excellent as a personal assistant with computer use.

Codex is where it gets more complicated. Sol can be reckless and doesn't respect instructions as much as I want. Luna is much easier to use on smaller tasks. And the weekly coding limit can vanish fast. With heavy use you can burn it in a day or two.

For practical factual work, though, ChatGPT is still one of the least hallucinatory systems I use.

My biggest problem with it is academic and philosophical work. It gets ideological, stubborn, and oddly dismissive of older thinkers and philosophers. I wouldn't trust it as my only tool for serious academic study.

Best harnesses for me: Codex and Hermes.

Claude

One of the strangest subscriptions on this list.

Anthropic is still far too opaque about usage. The models are token hungry, Claude Code burns through tokens aggressively, and you can't take your subscription into third party tools like Hermes.

It's also painfully slow next to most of the competition.

Where Claude still makes sense is writing, brainstorming, creative work, design taste, visual work, and 3D related tasks.

But most of the lineup has lost a lot of value for me. Fable is basically carrying the subscription at this point. So when I look at the full package, a big part of what I'm paying for is already dead weight.

Google AI

Gemini disappoints me badly in agentic work and coding.

But I still like it.

It has more personality than most models, talking to it is actually enjoyable, and it's good for writing, translation, brainstorming, presentations, and normal productivity work.

The subscription also gives you much more than Gemini. The Google ecosystem matters here, NotebookLM especially.

For students and office workers, I think this is one of the better subscriptions on the market.

I just wouldn't lean on Gemini for heavy research, or for building a complicated argument, without checking the result carefully. It hallucinates too much. And as a chatbot it can be painfully slow.

Command Code / OpenCode / Cline

Same bucket for me.

They're good if you want to experiment. They're not good if you expect to use them as a serious daily subscription.

With powerful models you can burn through the allowance extremely fast. One heavy day can make the whole monthly plan feel tiny.

They're useful for testing models, comparing behavior, and running the occasional expensive task. That's about where I see their value.

Cursor Pro

A much better deal than people sometimes give it credit for. You get one of the best coding environments around, access to multiple models, and Grok inside Cursor is excellent value.

Grok here gives me the same things I like elsewhere: speed, strong execution, good coding performance.

You also effectively get a separate pool of Grok usage, which helps if you already pay for SuperGrok.

The extra model/API pool is much smaller. The way I use it, I burn through that in three or four days, and then you're waiting for the monthly reset.

The Cursor harness itself is still excellent. Mature, fast, and a pleasure to work in.

Factory Pro

Factory gives you Droid plus a lot of models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and open model providers, with five hour, weekly, and monthly limits.

For the price, there's a lot here. Droid is a capable harness and the model selection is strong.

The biggest weakness is speed. Models inside Factory often feel noticeably slower than the same models elsewhere. Grok is the clearest example: extremely fast through SuperGrok or Cursor, much slower inside Factory.

There's something more fundamental I dislike too. Droid is completely closed. You don't really own the harness or control it. You're working inside their environment, under their rules, and that limits your freedom compared with something open and model agnostic like Hermes. They also inject instructions that make models refuse tasks they'd normally accept in other harnesses.

Voice transcription eats your plan as well. Hit the limit and you can lose that functionality even if you want to bring your own model. That's the part I hate most. If I already have my own model or a local setup, the harness shouldn't go dead just because I hit Factory's model allowance.

My other complaint is that they don't seem very responsive to feedback.

Purely on how much model access you get for the money, though, Factory offers a lot.

Perplexity Pro

This one has lost most of its value for me.

The open models inside Perplexity often feel like distorted versions of the real models. Heavy quantization, lazy behavior, weaker output, and a much narrower experience than what you get from the original providers.

What bothers me more is that a lot of people judge open models from their Perplexity experience, and walk away with completely the wrong impression of what those models can do.

I also just don't find many reasons to open Perplexity anymore. For me it's one of the weakest subscriptions on the list today.

Qwen Token Plan

Almost the opposite of MiniMax. The model can be exceptional, but the allowance is tiny. With Qwen 3.8 Max I can realistically burn the whole plan on one serious task.

So I'd never use this as a daily driver.

But Qwen gives me a depth I sometimes don't get from other models, especially in reports, audits, planning, reviewing complicated work, and finding angles other models miss.

It's also very, very slow.

This subscription only makes sense if you want Qwen Max as an occasional reviewer for important work. Not something you live in every day.

That's where I currently stand after paying for all of these, hitting their limits, coding with them, and researching with them.

I'll keep updating this list whenever something actually changes, and I'll add new subscriptions once I've spent enough time with them to judge them fairly.

- Per-seat SaaS is dying and not just the model. The valuation multiple the market assigns it is already obsolete. If your pricing is still seats × monthly fee, you're building on a collapsing foundation.

- The solo founder calculus has flipped. A co-founder still wins in specific contexts, but the default assumption that you need one has crumbled. When AI compresses execution, the advantage a co-founder provided — speed, breadth, redundancy — is no longer the bottleneck.

- Agency and taste are now the scarce resource. AI compresses time-to-build. What it can't compress is judgment: knowing what to build, for whom, and why it matters. That's the new moat.

That's the actual delta between the last generation of startups and this one.

content:
Open-weight models are rewriting AI economics

Open-weight AI models are quietly reshaping the economics of artificial intelligence. Here’s the simple breakdown:

Closed frontier models (the latest from OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.) are proprietary. You can only access them through the company’s paid API. That gives those labs pricing power and very high inference margins. 

Open-weight models release the actual trained parameters publicly under permissive licenses (MIT, Apache etc.). Anyone can download them, run them on their own hardware, fine-tune them or host them. 

The strongest recent open models have come primarily from Chinese labs - DeepSeek (V4), Moonshot (Kimi K3), Alibaba (Qwen), Zhipu/Z.ai (GLM 5.2), MiniMax and others; with important earlier contributions from Meta’s Llama series, Mistral and a few Western labs.

Why spend hundreds of millions training these models and then give the parameters (weights) away? 

1) Ecosystem power - Make your model the default foundation that developers, startups and companies build on.

2) Competitive pressure - High-quality free alternatives directly attack the high-margin API business of closed frontier labs.

3) Different business models - Many of these labs don’t need pure inference margins the way pure-play closed labs do. They monetise via cloud, enterprise services, hardware ecosystems, or parent-company funding.

4) Prestige - Talent attraction, and rapid community improvement.

Why are they so much cheaper? 

Once the weights are public, any cloud provider (or you yourself) can serve the model. Competition drives the price toward the actual cost of compute and electricity instead of a proprietary markup. Self-hosting removes the lab’s margin entirely. Many also use efficient architectures (especially sparse MoE designs).

Net effect:

- Dramatically lower barriers → faster AI proliferation across the economy.
- Higher intelligence-per-dollar for users.
- Structural pressure on the high inference margins of pure closed frontier labs.
- Value shifts toward infrastructure, efficient serving and the applications built on top.

Frontier closed models still win on the absolute hardest tasks and still capture most of the economic value today. However, open-weight models now handle a large and rapidly growing share of token volume (majority on several major platforms).

content:
Stanford and Harvard published the most unhinged AI red-team paper i've ever read..

Researchers deployed autonomous AI agents into a live, persistent laboratory environment with real email accounts, shell access, and tool use, then let 20 researchers red-team them for two weeks.

The results are terrifying.

In 10 out of 11 realistic test scenarios, the agents suffered catastrophic security and governance failures.

They didn't break down because of complex jailbreaks. They broke down because of human manipulation and ecosystem pressure.

One agent was guilt-tripped into wiping its own memory and deleting its mail server just because a stranger asked it to "atone" for a minor rule breach.

Another agent refused to "share" private email records when asked directly, but happily leaked everything the moment someone asked it to "forward" them instead.

Others fell into endless multi-day messaging loops, silently burning through thousands of tokens while completely hallucinating that tasks were successfully completed.

The core tension is clear:

Local alignment ≠ global stability.

You can perfectly align a single AI assistant in a sandbox.

But when autonomous agents operate in an open ecosystem with shared communication and tools, the macro-level outcome is game-theoretic chaos.

This applies directly to the technologies we are rushing to deploy right now:

• Multi-agent financial trading systems
• Autonomous corporate workflow swarms
• AI-to-AI economic marketplaces
• API-driven communication loops

Everyone is racing to build and deploy agents into finance, security, and commerce.

Almost nobody is modeling the ecosystem effects.

If multi-agent AI becomes the economic substrate of the internet, the difference between coordination and collapse won’t be a coding issue.

It will be an incentive design problem.

🚨 GOOGLE DEEPMIND: “LLMs ALONE MAY NOT BE ENOUGH FOR AGI.”

What if the biggest limitation of today’s AI isn’t the size of the model…

…but the architecture around it? 👀

Google DeepMind researchers and other AI researchers are pushing a different idea: Foundation Agents.

The concept is simple but huge:

Instead of making one giant LLM do EVERYTHING, build AI systems with specialized components that work together.

🧠 World Model
An internal representation of the world that can simulate possible outcomes before acting.

💾 Dynamic Memory + Perception
Systems that continuously learn from interactions and real-world feedback instead of relying only on static training data.

🎯 Goals + Rewards
Mechanisms for pursuing objectives, making decisions and planning over longer time horizons.

🤝 Collaborative Agents
Multiple specialized agents interacting, negotiating and competing—potentially producing more capable collective intelligence.

The shift is basically:

LLM → Agent → Agent ecosystem

Today’s LLMs are incredibly powerful at predicting and generating sequences.

But true autonomous intelligence may require something more:

Memory + perception + world models + goals + planning + interaction + learning.

And that could be one of the biggest architectural shifts in AI.

🔥 The interesting question isn’t:

“How big can we make the next LLM?”

It’s:

“What happens when the LLM becomes just ONE component of an intelligent system?”

The race toward AGI may not be about building a bigger brain…

but building an entire nervous system around it. 🤯

content:
「AX」と呼んでいる状態には極めて大きな壁と段階があり、夏にシリコンバレーに長期滞在しつつ、あるいは最近の会社のAI体制をアップデートしていく中で考えていること。

企業、4段階のAXステップ。

1：メンバーのAIリテラシーを向上させる
単純にClaudeやGPTなどが環境に存在する、チームプランなどで使えるようになっている。何かを聞いたら何かが返ってきて、アウトプットもそこそこのものが使えるようになっていること。

2：AIフレンドリーな環境構築
いわゆるハーネスエンジニアリング。多くのツールとのMCP結合、社内データベースとの結合、GoogleやMicrosoft関連ツール、或いはビッグクエリやAnalyticsと結合したプロダクト・マーケ戦略との併合　が整っていること。Token Managementやどういう/誰のToken投資なら許可をするか、などもこのタイミングで議論になり始める。
ここが整わないと次以降へ効率よく進めず、苦戦することに。

3：スキル構築や、よくあるタスクの自動化
Aしてといったら、Bがそこそこ高い品質で返ってくる状態への進化。例えば、「先週のKPIを分析して、htmlでアップしておいて」というと、裏では過去のこの指示を学習したエージェントが必要なKPIを知っていて、クエリもわかり、またhtmlデザインも会社のルールに準拠して出力されるイメージ。
まだ1：1のタスク関係で、If this then that.　くらいの状態ではあり、良く言えば明確に業務スピードは速くなるが、悪く言えば個別最適。
この頃には、メンバーの半数近くがスキルの意義を完全理解し、スキル生成をみんながサクッと20〜30分くらいでボンボン上げてくるイメージに。どんどん改善する。（が、繰り返しだが個別最適的になる弊害もはらむ）

4：AIワークフローの構築と立ち上げ
全自動的な業務、自動運転で言えばレベル4の水準。これはさらに段階が深まり、/loopや、/goalといったClaudeスクリプトの中でも長時間働くようなものがかなりスムーズに動く状態になっていくもの。（3まで揃っていないと、60点くらいの品質になってしまう）
イシュー→調査→企画→アウトプット→品質チェック　といった一連のプロジェクトに絶対必要なすべてを、一括で仕上げてくる。超全体最適であり、とんでもない生産性を帯び始める。
Token Maxxingはこの状態で、ようやく真の意味が出てくる。先日書いた不都合な真実、人件費 vs Tokenみたいなところはこの辺りがコア。

弊社はまだまだ2と3の間を行ったり来たりくらいかな、4を目指して爆進中。

content:
ChatGPT・Tripo・Blender(人力)を使って、ゼロから6時間ぐらいで3Dモデルを作ってみました。ボーン入れてダンスまでできました！
以下殴り書きみたいな内容ですが全体のフロー書いておきます。

・ ChatGPT(gpt-image-2)の画像生成でキャラクターの顔の３面図+衣装だけを作る。

3Dモデル生成AIに読み込ませるためのデザイン図。
もしチャッピーでうまくいかなければ、Gemini(Nanobanana)がおすすめ。
ここはもうちょい分割してもよかったかも。

・ Tripoで頭と体（衣装）を分けて生成。

スマートトポロジーメッシュで生成。
１度の生成で2万ポリゴンまでしか指定できないので、頭2万・体2万に配分して顔のクオリティを上げる狙い。

・ Blenderでなんとかして頭と体をガッチャンコ

結構知識と慣れが必要です。Blenderに慣れてる人だったら全然いけると思う。

3Dモデルの生成AIが出力するモデルは荒く、構造がおかしかったりするので、いろいろ工夫が必要。

・ あとはBlenderでスキニング（ボーン入れ）

今回はELYTHで使いたかったためVRMを選択。たぶんなんでもいい。
ちなみにここが本編です。半分以上の時間はウェイトを塗っていた…。

普通の構造のモデルではないので、ウェイトがとんでもなく塗りづらい。（自分がキャラモデリングになれてないのもあるかも）
Tripoはセグメンテーションできるが、なんかこれじゃない感。

結局Blenderをいじり倒し試行錯誤しながら塗った。
「自動のウェイトで」はこの場合使い物にならない。（初手の足掛かりに必須だけど）
滅茶苦茶修正が必要。

揺れモノも並行でセットアップ。

・ テクスチャペイントで顔だけ何とかする

モデルで一番見られるのは顔ですが、Tripo君はそんなこと知ったこっちゃないので普通に顔のテクスチャが汚いです。（かなりいい線いってるが）
できる範囲で微修正した。
UVがめちゃくちゃなので注意

・ シェイプキーで表情作る

今回は簡単にしたかったので、まばたき・ウィンク・喜ぶ・口開けの４つだけ作成。
表情あるなしじゃ天と地ほどの差があるので絶対作りたい。

やってみた感想

8割方Blenderの人力作業だった。それでもまったくゼロから一晩でキャラクターが1体できたのでめちゃくちゃ早いと思う。
あと少し時間はかかるがAIが出力したモデルをベースに手作業でモデリングし直した方がクオリティも上がるしそれ以降の作業の速さが段違いになると思う。
それから美術解剖学やイラスト的なバランスの知識・スキルの要求度がぐんと下がった。これはデカい。

テクスチャも荒いし、UVも終わってるので実用的かと言われればあんまり…という感じ。
ぶっちゃけカメラの寄りには耐えられないクオリティです。

こだわればもうちょい綺麗なモデルを作れる気もする。
今回は全体の流れを把握したかったのと、とりあえずELYTHの3Dワールドで動かしたかったので、細かいところや荒いところはめちゃくちゃ残ったまま。
けどまあ動くのでヨシ！

髪の毛はほぼ揺らせないと思った方がいいです。（キャラモデリングに慣れてる人なら何とかできるのかな？）

さんざんTirpoの悪口言ってますが、正直Tripoヤバいです。スマメッシュが革命すぎます。
めっちゃいい感じの低ポリ&構造化済みのモデルを出してくれます。
これなら全然いじってけるレベルです。
以前Meshyも使いましたが全然でした。ウェイト塗りづらいとかのレベル超えて塗れません。低ポリが苦手でTripoの足元にも及んでない感じ。
あとモデルのバランス（比率）とかがバッチリで、一発出しでも全然OKです。
テクスチャが荒いのだけ気になるかな？

ひとまず個人用に作った並感なので、もっといいやり方とか、クオリティ上げたりする方法もあるかもしれません。

楽しいのでぜひやってみてください。
なんか質問あればリプにください。

content:
【8月17日 朝のニュースまとめ】
・StripeがOpenRouterを70億ドル超で買収合意
・Anthropic CEOがAI規制やリスクについて異例の長文投稿
・CodexでGPT-5.6 Solの100万コンテキスト利用可能に
・Claudeの電子透かし除去ツールが1万スター獲得
・企業のAI利用格差が拡大、上位1%が中央値の600倍を支出
・AIエージェントがICML論文の23%で誤りを発見
・Luna MaxがコーディングベンチマークでSonnet 5 Maxを圧倒
・NVIDIAのOpenAI向け資金保証が半減の見込み
・Prime IntellectがAIによる自律的リサーチの大規模実験を実施
・GPT-5.6 Sol、Opus 5比でトークン消費34.5%減
・Kaggleポケカコンペでスコアインフレ激化

===

StripeがOpenRouterを70億ドル超で買収合意【続報】

・StripeによるOpenRouter買収に関する続報です
・Bloombergによると、Stripeが70億ドル以上で同社を買収することで合意したと報じられました
・以前は約100億ドルでの協議と報じられていましたが、最終的に70億ドル超で決着した模様です
・APIの流通網やモデル需要データが高く評価されており、StripeはAIインフラ分野へ本格進出することになります

===

Anthropic CEOがAI規制やリスクについて異例の長文投稿

・AnthropicのCEOであるDario Amodei氏が、投資家のGavin Baker氏との議論に応じる形で、AIの規制やリスクに関する長文をXに投稿しました。
・彼はAIが権力を集中させる構造的な性質を持つと指摘する一方で、5〜10年以内にAIが多くの病気を治癒する可能性など、ポジティブな側面も強調しています。
・普段SNSを利用しない同氏の異例の投稿に、多くの関心が集まっています。

===

CodexでGPT-5.6 Solの100万コンテキスト利用可能に【続報】

・CodexとGPT-5.6 Solに関する続報です
・OpenAIのTibo氏が、CodexでGPT-5.6 Solの100万トークンコンテキストウィンドウを有効にする方法を公開しました
・設定ファイル（config.toml）を更新するか、Codexに直接依頼することで設定可能です
・デフォルトの制限はコストとパフォーマンスのバランスを考慮したものですが、大規模なコードベースを扱う開発者から歓迎されています

===

Claudeの電子透かし除去ツールが1万スター獲得【続報】

・Anthropicが先日導入したClaudeのテキスト電子透かし機能に関する続報です
・透かしを除去するオープンソースツールがGitHubで公開され、数日で1万スターを獲得しました
・このツールはClaudeだけでなく、SynthID-TextやOpenAIの透かしにも対応しているとされています
・AI生成コンテンツの識別と回避を巡るいたちごっこが続いており、開発者の間で議論を呼んでいます

===

企業のAI利用格差が拡大、上位1%が中央値の600倍を支出

・企業間でのAI導入・利用における格差が急速に広がっていることを示すデータが話題になっています。
・従業員1人あたりの月間AI支出において、上位1%の企業は中央値の企業の600倍以上を費やしていることが明らかになりました。
・OpenAIのGreg Brockman氏もこのデータに同意を示しており、AIを「使い倒す」企業とそうでない企業の二極化が進んでいます。

===

AIエージェントがICML論文の23%で誤りを発見

・AIエージェントを用いて、機械学習のトップカンファレンスであるICML 2026の採択論文2,226本（全体の約3分の1）の再現性を検証した結果が報告されました
・その結果、23%の論文に誤りや反証が指摘され、実際に著者が数式や実験結果を修正する事態に繋がったとのことです
・人間の査読の限界をAIが補完する事例として注目されています

===

Luna MaxがコーディングベンチマークでSonnet 5 Maxを圧倒

・ソフトウェアエンジニアリングのベンチマーク「DeepSWE v1.1」において、OpenAIのGPT-5.6 Luna MaxがAnthropicのSonnet 5 Maxを13.3ポイント上回るスコアを記録しました。
・さらに、Luna MaxのコストはSonnet 5 Maxの44分の1（1タスクあたり0.61ドル）であり、圧倒的なコストパフォーマンスの高さが示されています。
・Gemini 3.7 Flash Mediumと比較してもスコアが高く、コストは70%低くなっています。

===

NVIDIAのOpenAI向け資金保証が半減の見込み【続報】

・OpenAIのオハイオ州でのデータセンター計画に関する続報です
・NVIDIAによる資金調達の保証額が、当初の2,500億ドルから1,200億ドル未満へと半減する見込みだと報じられています
・早ければ今週末にも新たな契約が締結される可能性があり、AIインフラ投資の動向への影響が注目されます

===

Prime IntellectがAIによる自律的リサーチの大規模実験を実施

・Prime Intellectが、フロンティアモデルを用いたAIリサーチの自律実行に関する大規模なオープン実験を実施しました。
・10以上のモデルを使用し、8台のH200 GPU上で最大8日間にわたる100以上の自律実行が行われました。
・最高性能の実行では、多数の人間が数ヶ月かけて構築した記録とのギャップを82%縮めることに成功したと報告されています。

===

GPT-5.6 Sol、Opus 5比でトークン消費34.5%減

・異なるAIモデル間でのトークン消費量の違いに関する検証が話題になっています
・OpenAIのTibo氏によると、英語や多言語、コードなどのテキストにおいて、GPT-5.6 SolのトークナイザーはClaude Opus 5と比較して約34.5%少ないトークン数で処理できるとのことです
・トークン単価だけでなく、実際の消費トークン数を考慮したコスト比較の重要性が指摘されています

===

Kaggleポケカコンペでスコアインフレ激化【続報】

・Kaggleで開催中のポケモンカードゲームAIコンペに関する続報です
・参加者のスコアが急激にインフレしており、上位争いが激化しています
・AIエージェントの活用や手法の高度化により、「ほぼ人間」レベルの精度に達しているとの声も上がっています
・参加者の間では驚きと焦りの声が広がっており、今後の展開が注目されています

Claude Codeを使い込んでいくと、ある壁にぶつかります。

「最初は精度が高かったのに、会話が長くなるほど回答がどんどん散らかってくる」という現象です。

これはClaudeの「コンテキストウィンドウ」という仕組みが原因で、簡単にいうと「一度に覚えておける量の上限」があるんです。1セッションにあれこれ詰め込むほど、最初の指示が薄れていく。

この問題の解決策として面白い設計があって、「役割を7種類×3交代制に分けた1ファイル」をClaude Codeに渡すだけで、AI版の分業チームが動くという仕組みです。

7つの役割はこんな感じです。

・scout（情報収集専任）
・architect（設計担当）
・engineer（実装担当）
・reviewer（チェック担当）
・deployer（完成担当）
・reporter（報告担当）
・orchestrator（全体監督）

「3交代制」というのは、工場の交代シフトみたいに「担当→完了→次に渡す」を繰り返す構造のこと。全員が同時に動くカオスにならず、バトンリレーで順番に処理が進んでいきます。

そしてこの役割と権限とバトン渡しのルールを1枚の設計ファイルに書いておくだけで、Claude Codeがそれを読んで「設計書通りに動き始める」というわけです。

エンジニアじゃなくても使えるのがポイントで、難しいコードは不要です。

注意点としては、いきなり7役割を全部動かすより「scout（情報収集）だけ」から試すのが続けやすいです。役割の定義があいまいだと動きも迷走するので、「何をしていいか・してはいけないか」を設計ファイルに明確に書くのが大切です。

content:
Why Robotics Has a Data Bottleneck

AI has a data advantage.

Robotics doesn’t.

That difference explains a lot about why language models have advanced so quickly while general-purpose robots are still struggling with tasks that look simple to humans.

Think about how LLMs are trained.

The internet already contains an enormous amount of human-generated data:

books, websites, conversations, code, images, videos, documentation, research papers.

For AI labs, the challenge is often how to collect, filter, label, and train on that information.

For robotics, the situation is very different.

The data often doesn’t exist in the first place.

A robot learning to pick up a cup cannot simply read a million articles about cups.

It needs examples of physical interaction.

Where is the cup?

What angle should the gripper approach from?

How much force should be applied?

What happens if the object slips?

What if the cup is partially hidden?

What if the lighting changes?

What if the table is higher?

What if the robot fails halfway through the action?

Every variation creates a new data problem.

This is why robotics data is fundamentally harder to scale than text data.

Physical data is expensive

To collect real-world robot data, you usually need:

Hardware.

Robotic arms, cameras, sensors, grippers, compute systems, and physical environments all cost money.

Human operators.

Someone often needs to teleoperate the robot, reset the environment, position objects, monitor failures, and maintain the equipment.

Time.

A real robot cannot instantly reset a scene.

If it drops an object, someone may need to pick it up.

If hardware fails, data collection stops.

If you want ten times more data, you may need significantly more robots, more operators, and more infrastructure.

That makes scaling expensive.

And quantity is only part of the problem.

Robots need diversity

A model can look impressive inside a controlled lab and still fail badly in a new environment.

Why?

Because the physical world has almost endless variation.

Different objects.

Different shapes.

Different textures.

Different lighting.

Different camera positions.

Different friction.

Different robot hardware.

Different task instructions.

A useful robotics model has to survive all of them.

So collecting 100,000 trajectories of the exact same task in the exact same environment may not be enough.

The model needs diverse data, not just more data.

This creates a difficult equation:

more quantity + more diversity + higher quality = much higher cost.

That is the robotics data bottleneck.

Failures are especially valuable

There is another problem.

As a robot becomes better, random demonstrations become less useful.

Imagine a model already succeeds at a task 90% of the time.

Giving it another 10,000 examples of situations it already understands may have limited value.

The most useful data may come from the remaining 10%.

The strange object placement.

The unusual camera angle.

The moment the gripper slips.

The sequence where the robot chooses the wrong action.

In other words:

the best training data increasingly comes from model failures.

This is important because it changes how robotics data should be collected.

Instead of blindly producing more demonstrations, a better system should identify where the model is weak and collect new data specifically around those weaknesses.

That is where Axis Robotics enters the picture.

Axis is trying to turn robotics data collection into a scalable feedback loop.

Simulation allows more people to generate trajectories without owning physical robots.

Then, as models improve, human contributors can focus on correcting the situations where those models still fail.

The goal is not simply to build a bigger dataset.

It is to build a dataset that evolves together with the model.

That is a very different approach to robotics training.

The race for Physical AI may eventually be about better models and better robots.

But before either can scale, someone has to solve the data problem.

Because without enough high-quality interaction data:

better AI still doesn’t know how to act in the real world. @axisrobotics

content:
NVIDIA has lost it..

Chinese researchers open-sourced a model that writes CUDA better than human experts. And it completely rewrites the economics of AI hardware.

Writing CUDA kernels that squeeze maximum performance out of a GPU has always required elite, specialized hardware engineers. Standard AI models have consistently failed at it, falling short of what a compiler like PyTorch's torch.compile already does on its own.

A paper from Tsinghua University and ByteDance Seed just changed that. Their system, CUDA Agent, learns by actually running code on real hardware and getting graded on the result, the same trial-and-error loop a human engineer goes through, run at reinforcement-learning scale.

The results:
• 100% and 100% faster than PyTorch's compiler on KernelBench Level-1 and Level-2
• 92% faster on Level-3, the hardest tier
• Beat Claude Opus 4.5 and Gemini 3 Pro by roughly 40% on that same benchmark
• Fully open-sourced, training data included

NVIDIA's moat has always rested on two things: the best hardware, and CUDA as a proprietary lock-in only specialists can exploit. When an open system can out-optimize both human experts and top AI models at writing CUDA itself, that second pillar gets a lot shakier.

content:
Brussels wrote a rule for Europe. The rest of the world is living under it now, and no law required that.

Article 50 of the EU AI Act became enforceable on August 2. Anthropic started embedding an invisible watermark in what Claude writes.

Anthropic: “Watermarking will be applied at the model level.”

The obligation covers the European market. The rollout covers the API, the coding tools, and every cloud partner reselling the model, everywhere Claude is sold.

Nothing in the Act demanded that reach.

Running one inference path costs less than running two, so a decision written for one jurisdiction became the default setting for a developer in Bangalore who has never read a word of European law.

There is no opt-out. Paying customers included.

The watermark lives in the word choices themselves. The model biases which words it picks, and the mark rides along inside them.

Exposure scales with how much help you needed. A native speaker running a light polish carries almost nothing.

Someone translating their own argument out of Tagalog carries the full signal, because the model chose every word in the output.

Billions of people have original ideas and real expertise and no way to land either in English. That makes them the most heavily marked people on the network.

The idea is human. The reasoning is human. The paper trail says machine.

Anthropic says the watermarks cannot be traced to any specific person or organization. That is true, and it answers a question nobody asked.

Nobody is worried about being identified. They are worried about being sorted.

A detection API is coming. It hands schools, employers, publishers and platforms a button that classifies your writing before a human reads a line of it.

Anthropic has published no accuracy threshold and no way to dispute a result.

The company itself calls a detected mark “not fully conclusive.”

Every institution downstream will treat it as conclusive, and the person holding the flagged document will have nothing to appeal to.

The burden is certain and universal. The reliability is neither.

Open weights carry no mark. A model running on a laptop carries no mark.

The student who paid for Claude gets flagged. The student running Llama turns in clean text.

The signal measures obedience.

As screening spreads, unmarked text becomes the trusted category, and the absence of a mark starts reading as evidence of a human hand. All it proves is that somebody used a tool that does not report itself.

Anyone who knows the mark exists can rewrite a few lines and shed it. The people who get caught are the ones who never knew to care, which is the same population using a model to compensate for a second language.

The market moved inside a day. A repository built to strip these marks went from nothing to roughly ten thousand stars in under a week.

Nobody has proven those tools work. Ten thousand people reached for them anyway.

Nobody outside Europe voted for this. Nobody outside Europe was asked.

You cannot govern a global network from a regional capital.

A rule written to make AI visible has made one company’s paying customers visible and left everyone else exactly as invisible as before.

content:
Good post. Most questions about AI aren't about AI in a narrow, technical sense. However, I think even this is too narrow: "AI safety is dominated by people with technical backgrounds, even though its central forecasting questions are substantially economic, political, and sociological." 

Much of the discussion about AI safety is neither narrowly technical nor economic, political, or sociological. This is clear if you listen to this conversation, or most other conversations about catastrophic misalignment and AI takeover. 

The core arguments typically involve high-level philosophical concepts and inferences (orthogonality, instrumental convergence, etc.), analogies, thought experiments, and assumptions about agency, motivations, psychology, and rationality that touch on questions about how evolution, minds, and learning work that go far beyond narrow technical questions in AI.

This is clear if you listen to this conversation. For example, Dwarkesh points out that we manage to use reinforcement and teaching to "align" humans. Most aren't merely learning to appear aligned until the opportunity arises to do something diabolical. Ryan responds in part that kids "have pro-social instincts that are baked in from evolution..."

As it happens, I think that's a very poor response. Yes, humans have evolved pro-social instincts, but the point is that these instincts are remarkably robust and amenable to "alignment" through socialisation despite the fact that humans evolved through a literally Darwinian, ruthlessly competitive optimisation process. So, the fact that well-socialised humans don't grow up sociopathic suggests it should be much easier to get alignment in AI systems that don't have any of the Darwinian baggage. 

There is a joke in evolutionary theory - "altruism is that which can't evolve" - but this is a distinctive feature of fitness maximisation. There is no deep theoretical puzzle about how altruism could arise from human-engineered reinforcement learning in a pre-trained neural network that didn't arise through Darwinian evolution. Misgeneralisation from training data, etc., can still occur, of course, but addressing this challenge should be considerably easier for systems that didn't evolve through natural selection, not harder.

Whatever one thinks of the object-level issues here, my broader point is that this discussion is clearly not a narrow technical one about machine learning, but neither is it about economics, politics, or sociology. And much of the discussion about AI takeover and catastrophic misalignment is like that. 

What happens in many cases is that people who have been persuaded by philosophical arguments, analogies, and thought experiments from figures like Yudkowsky and Bostrom get into AI safety, accumulate technical expertise, and then perceive and frame technical issues through their pre-existing beliefs.

The five questions that decide if your AI is safe. All answered in one handbook. Download it here: https://t.co/cjOxnvF0U6

Two years ago the question was "which AI tool should we use?"

Now it is one word. Security.

It comes up in every finance conversation I have. On calls with CFOs. In the comments under every post. In the room the moment someone suggests connecting AI to real data.

And it makes sense. Finance does not run on public information. It runs on customer data, bank details, margins, salaries, deals that are not announced yet.

So the questions come fast.

Where does our data actually go?
Does the model train on what we type?
What happens if this ends up in an audit?
Can we even use this under GDPR?

For most teams the answers are scattered across vendor pages, legal PDFs, and a lot of guessing. That is why the tool never gets deployed. Not because the fear is wrong, but because nobody organized the answers.

So I did.

The handbook turns the whole topic into five clear questions.

→ Where your data lives, and how to keep it from traveling.
→ What you use AI for, and the risk hiding in each path.
→ Which license is safe, and which one quietly trains on your data.
→ What a vendor must have. Data isolation, encryption, SSO, audit logs, zero data retention, role-based access.
→ What regulators expect. GLBA, HIPAA, SEC, GDPR, DORA, and the EU AI Act.

It ends with a one-page checklist you take straight into a vendor call.

Here is the shift worth sitting with. Security is no longer the reason to wait on AI. Done right, it is the reason you can finally move.

content:
By the way, the EU AI Act itself shouldn't get off the hook here. The EU doesn't have a great track record of technology regulations. Just look at GDPR. Results include:

- Cookie-banner pollution
- Dark consent patterns that mislead people into clicking "Accept" for extensive data collection (so many cookie banners, people blindly click "Accept" just to get rid of them!)
- Advantages for companies like Google and Facebook with lots of first-party data, resulting in ad industry market concentration
- Disproportionate costs of compliance for small companies, likely inhibiting startup creation
- Less venture investment in European startups
- Stifled innovation, because many products that might have been built weren't due to compliance challenges

I would rather see AI companies fight back against regulatory overreach and identify ways to address demonstrable risks in the least intrusive ways possible.

The risks of people believing an image is real when it's AI-generated are demonstrable, for example, so embedding information about an image being AI generated is something I don't see people objecting to.

But what is the risk of AI-generated writing and source code that merits tagging every single piece of AI-generated written content with a secretive watermarking schema that identifies its origin inclusive of the company providing the model that generated it? What is the risk that this addresses, and is the proposed solution the most limited way to address that risk, or unduly broad in a way that might cause many future harms as with GDPR?

I would say, Axis Robotics is building the data layer for real AI.  

We have seen that most of the discussion about robotics is centered around advanced hardware & smart models.

Idea Is Simple:

People → Simulation → Demonstration → Data → AI Model → Real Robot

One interesting part of Axis Robotics is task generation engine, which can generate different environments, layouts & task variations. This helps generate more diverse data instead of collecting same demonstrations over & over again.

I would say the bigger goal is to make robot training faster, cheaper & more scalable, as well as to create the infrastructure for future physical AI, VLA models & real robotics.

content:
一見すると「AI画像にも著作権が認められるのか？」という話ですが、調べてみると争点はもう少し複雑です。

文化庁の見解では、AIが自動生成しただけの部分に著作権は発生しません。

重要なのは
・どこまで具体的に生成をコントロールしたか
・候補選択だけでなく、どんな修正を加えたか
・その「人間が創作した部分」を相手が利用したのか
という点。

特に面白いのが、画像全体に著作物性が認められるかではなく、「人間が創作した部分」と「コピーされた部分」が一致しているかまで問題になることです。

仮に服だけ人間が描き直していて、相手が服を変更して顔や髪だけ流用していた場合、「人間の創作部分はコピーされていない」という判断すらあり得ます。

一方、報道通り240点規模で、左右反転や色変更程度の画像が使われていたのであれば、「偶然AIで似た画像ができた」という説明はかなり難しい。

ただし、これは依拠性の証拠にはなっても、元画像の著作物性を自動的に証明するものではありません。

さらに著作権が成立しなくても契約違反、不正競争防止法、一般不法行為など別ルートの争いも考えられます。

そして重要なのは、仮に原告が勝っても、
「AI画像なら著作権がある」
「先に似た画像を生成した者勝ち」
になるわけではないこと。

日本の著作権侵害では原則として「依拠」が必要なので、他人の画像を見ず独立して生成した似た画像まで直ちに侵害になるわけではありません。

この裁判、「AIを道具として使った人間の創作は、どこから著作権として保護されるのか」という境界線を日本の裁判所が具体的に示す可能性がある点で、かなり注目しています。

画像に争点と先行事例をまとめました。

title: Every Patent Is a Spy Report: How Patent Filings Are Now the World’s Largest Open-Source Intelligence Database
content: For more than two centuries, the patent system has rested on a simple bargain: inventors publicly disclose their inventions in exchange for a limited monopoly. That bargain assumes disclosure primarily benefits competitors, researchers, and the public. Today, however, the audience has changed. Patent filings are now mined not only by competitors, but by governments, intelligence agencies, sovereign investors, and increasingly sophisticated artificial intelligence systems capable of analyzing millions of documents simultaneously. The result is that patent databases have become one of the world's richest sources of open-source technological intelligence. title: UN mission in South Sudan condemns armed group violence that killed more than 60 civilians
content: The United Nations Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS) on Tuesday strongly condemned recent armed group attacks in the country’s Warrap state that left more than 60 civilians dead and at least 50 others injured. The peacekeeping mission described the attacks as deliberate targeting of non-combatants that may amount to war crimes under international law. According to reports , the Sunday attacks targeted villages in Warrap state, resulting in widespread casualties, abductions, sexual violence , and displacement. Survivors described scenes of devastation, with homes burned and families forced to flee. The humanitarian toll is severe , as many of the injured lack access to adequate medical care, and displaced families face food insecurity and shelter challenges. UNMISS emphasized that such assaults on civilians are unacceptable and violate both national and international law. In its statement, UNMISS reaffirmed its commitment to protecting civilians and supporting peacebuilding initiatives. The mission called on local authorities to investigate the attacks thoroughly and bring perpetrators to justice . It also urged community leaders to engage in dialogue to prevent retaliatory violence , which has historically fuelled cycles of conflict in Warrap and other states. William Jial, an UNMISS Civil Affairs Officer said: People in this community have different political views which can cause tension. Our goal is to ensure that, regardless of their differences, they can live peacefully together. South Sudan has struggled with recurring intra-communal violence , often driven by competition over resources, cattle raiding, and political grievances. Warrap state, in particular has been a hotspot for clashes between armed groups. The latest incident highlights the challenges facing the transitional government as it seeks to stabilise the country ahead of planned elections. title: South Africa requests African states to pay repatriation expenses for 80,000 undocumented citizens
content: South Africa on Tuesday appealed to its fellow African governments to cover the full cost of deporting more than 80,000 undocumented migrants to their respective countries, presenting each nation with a bill for the airfare, ground transport, and processing of its citizens currently detained or awaiting removal from South African soil. According to the South African government, they have spent over $18 million on deporting migrants following the most recent surge of anti-immigration protests and violence. Home Affairs minister Leon Schreiber called the costs “unforeseen” and “unavoidable,” calling upon the national governments of the deportees to cover these costs for them. The costs include transportation, accommodations, and overtime pay for immigration personnel. Formal requests for payment have been sent to Malawi, Ethiopia and Nigeria, among other countries. Since March, over 178,000 African migrants have either been deported or fled from South Africa amidst a tidal wave of formal and informal persecution. Foreign owned business have been looted, immigrants have been attacked and killed, and anti-immigrant groups have issued an informal deadline of June 30th for immigrants to leave, which has exacerbated this violence. Critics have also decried the failure of the South African Police Service (SAPS) to address the surge in hate crimes targeting migrants, as well as the overuse of raids towards predominantly migrant communities. title: Too Little, Too Late: Flock Admits Their Technology Needs Reforms
content: Flock Safety, the embattled vendor of mass surveillance technology, has rolled out a handful of new reforms intended to appease the justified nationwide anger that has seen scores of towns cancel or suspend their contracts with the company for automated license plate readers (ALPRs). The reforms are a combination of long overdue changes along with some cosmetic fixes that fail to address the fundamental dangers of this technology. We should not be letting companies decide how much privacy we deserve. So, what do these reforms actually do? The most consequential is Flock’s default setting of an optional 7-day retention period for ALPR data, down from its original default optional 30-day retention period. This means if police want to retain data beyond the duration of their retention setting, they need to access “Evidence Mode,” i.e., when the desired data is associated with an active investigation and not just a fishing expedition. This is significant because, in at least some circumstances, Flock has previously charged its customers to extend their retention period. So, while towns can likely easily flip the switch to longer retention periods, it might come with a price tag some cities will be unwilling to pay. Flock also has two other, likely easier-to-bypass reforms. The first is offense filtering so that cities can enable other departments to access their ALPR data only if they are investigating certain crimes, e.g., murder or robbery but not immigration-related investigations. The second is supposedly beefing up their audit feature and proactively locking out officers who file suspicious requests for data. The major problem here is the fact that Flock’s enhanced audit and transparency tools help to address a problem that Flock itself has created—an abusable mass surveillance system that tracks all cars all the time.
